sentence: We prove a cell entropy inequality for a class of high order discontinuous Galerkin finite element methods approximating conservation laws, which implies convergence for the one dimensional scalar convex case.
scheme: Semi-discrete DG of Cockburn and Shu without slope limiting, Sec. 2 eq. (2.1) (OCR partly garbled; read as): find u(.,t) in V_h such that for all v in V_h and all I_j = (x_{j-1/2}, x_{j+1/2}): int_{I_j} u_t(x,t) v(x) dx + h_{j+1/2}(t) v(x^-_{j+1/2}) - h_{j-1/2}(t) v(x^+_{j-1/2}) - int_{I_j} f(u(x,t)) v_x(x) dx = 0. V_h = piecewise polynomials of degree up to r (an (r+1)-th order method), discontinuous across element interfaces (Sec. 1). h_{j+1/2}(t) = h(u(x^-_{j+1/2},t), u(x^+_{j+1/2},t)) is a Lipschitz continuous monotone flux (non-decreasing in the first argument, non-increasing in the second) or more generally an E-flux, eq. (2.2): (h(u^-,u^+) - f(u))(u^+ - u^-) <= 0 for all u between u^- and u^+. Entropy: square entropy U(u) = u^2/2 (Sec. 2 heading and eq. (2.9)). Conservation law (1.1): u_t + div f(u) = 0.

hypotheses.text: The entropy inequality proved is for the square entropy U(u) = u^2/2 only; for a general convex entropy only an inequality modulo an interpolation error term (2.12) is obtained, motivating an h-dependent modification (2.13).
h is a Lipschitz continuous monotone flux, or more generally an E-flux (2.2).

The scheme in Sec. 2 is the semi-discrete (continuous in time) form; for the theta time discretization (3.1)-(3.2) a sufficient condition for the cell entropy inequality is theta >= 1/2 (Crank-Nicolson to backward Euler).
Convergence: 'if f(u) is convex and we use the nonlinear limiting [3] to obtain a total variation boundedness for the solution, we will have convergence towards the unique entropy solution.'
Limiters must be projections P that do not increase the L2 norm of any degree-r polynomial in a cell, (3.8), to keep the inequality.

quantifier: every polynomial degree r (every order) of the DG method; every Lipschitz monotone or E-flux; convergence part: 1D scalar convex flux
justification: The cell entropy inequality for the square entropy is proved in Sec. 2 for the semi-discrete scheme (2.1) with any monotone or E-flux and any degree r (eqs. (2.5)-(2.9)); the proof uses only the E-flux property. Read alone, the sentence does not say that the inequality is for one entropy only, that convergence further needs a total variation bound from the nonlinear limiter of [3], or which time discretization is meant; the unlimited high-order method is not shown to converge, so the convergence half is not settled by the sentence alone. With the stated hypotheses (convex f, TVB via the limiter, limiter satisfying (3.8), semi-discrete or theta >= 1/2) the paper's argument is: TVB compactness plus Lax-Wendroff gives a weak solution, and one strictly convex entropy inequality with convex flux selects the entropy solution. The paper states this implication rather than proving it in full; we accept it as TRUE with hypotheses on the strength of that argument.

sentence: We have shown that the discontinuous Galerkin method, or equivalent Hermite type finite difference method, which evolves the whole polynomial inside a cell, satisfies a cell entropy inequality for the square entropy in multi space dimensions.
scheme: Semi-discrete DG of Sec. 2, eq. (2.1) (see item :01 for the 1D form, with monotone/E-flux (2.2)); in multi-D the scheme is (1.3): int_K u_t v dx + sum_{e in dK} int_e f(u).n v ds - int_K f(u).grad v dx = 0 on a triangulation T_h of triangles, tetrahedra or other simple elements, with the trace of f(u).n replaced by a monotone or E-flux. The Hermite finite-difference form for r = 1 evolves the mean and the slope, (2.14)-(2.15) (OCR garbled; formulas not readable).

hypotheses.text: Square entropy U(u) = u^2/2 (scalar conservation law).
Monotone flux or E-flux (2.2) at cell interfaces.
Multi-D: 'The same entropy inequality can be obtained for multi-space dimensions with arbitrary triangulations ... We omit the derivation detail since it parallels that for the one dimensional case.'
Semi-discrete in time; fully discrete only for theta >= 1/2 (Sec. 3) and a leap-frog variant (3.9)-(3.10).

quantifier: this one method family (DG of any degree on any triangulation), all dimensions, with monotone/E-flux
justification: Sec. 2 proves (2.9) for the semi-discrete 1D scheme; the multi-D statement is asserted with the derivation omitted as parallel to 1D (the same test-function choice v = u and an E-flux argument on each face). 'The square entropy' makes the scalar reading the default one. The paper does not prove the inequality for explicit fully discrete versions; the sentence names 'the discontinuous Galerkin method', which in this paper is the semi-discrete scheme (2.1). We rate it TRUE in both readings, noting the multi-D derivation is not printed.

sentence: Limiters to enforce total variation or maximum norm stability can be designed not to destroy this cell entropy inequality.
scheme: Fully discrete theta scheme (3.1)-(3.2) applied to the DG method (2.1) (OCR garbled; read as: int_{I_j} (u^{n+1} - u^n)/dt v dx + h^{n+theta}_{j+1/2} v(x^-_{j+1/2}) - h^{n+theta}_{j-1/2} v(x^+_{j-1/2}) - int_{I_j} f(u^{n+theta}) v_x dx = 0, with u^{n+theta} = (1-theta) u^n + theta u^{n+1}), followed by a limiter applied as a projection u^{n+1} = P u-tilde^{n+1}. Condition (3.8): int_{I_j} (P w)^2 dx <= int_{I_j} w^2 dx for every polynomial w of degree up to r; sufficient: writing w = sum a_l p_l and P w = sum b_l p_l in scaled Legendre polynomials, |b_l| <= |a_l| for all l.

hypotheses.text: Time discretization theta >= 1/2 (implicit, Crank-Nicolson to backward Euler) for the fully discrete inequality (3.6).

The limiter is a projection P that does not increase the cell L2 norm of any degree-r polynomial, (3.8); |b_l| <= |a_l| suffices and is 'easily checked to be correct for the P1 case (r = 1) in [3] and also for the general P_k case with similar minmod limiters'.
Square entropy only.

quantifier: some limiters (there exist limiters of minmod type with the stated property)
justification: With the hypotheses: Sec. 3 shows that any projection satisfying (3.8) keeps (3.6) for the theta >= 1/2 schemes, and that minmod-type limiters on the Legendre coefficients satisfy |b_l| <= |a_l|, hence (3.8); the total variation / maximum norm stability of those limiters is from the cited works [3], [4]. Read alone, the sentence suggests this works for the schemes those limiters are normally used with (explicit Runge-Kutta, as in [3]); the paper does not show the entropy inequality for explicit RK time stepping (only theta >= 1/2 and a leap-frog variant), and whether the TVB property of the limiter of [3] holds together with implicit theta stepping is not addressed here. So alone UNSURE.

sentence: We also consider two improvements which we label ENO-LLF (local Lax-Friedrichs) and ENO-Roe, which yield sharper shock transitions, improved overall accuracy, and for lower computational cost than previous implementation of the ENO schemes.
scheme: Conservative semi-discrete scheme (1.8a): L(u)_j = -(1/dx)(fhat_{j+1/2} - fhat_{j-1/2}) with consistent flux fhat(u,...,u) = f(u) (1.8b), advanced by the r-th order TVD Runge-Kutta scheme (1.6) under CFL lambda = dt/dx <= C_r lambda_0 (1.7b). ENO-Roe (Algorithm 2.1, Sec. 2): build the divided-difference table of H with H[x_{l-1/2}, x_{l+1/2}] = f(u(x_l)) and higher differences (2.4); start the stencil at k_min = j if the Roe speed a_{j+1/2} = (f(u_{j+1}) - f(u_j))/(u_{j+1} - u_j) > 0, else k_min = j+1 (2.5); grow the interpolating polynomial Q one point at a time, adding on the side whose divided difference has the smaller absolute value (2.7)-(2.9); fhat_{j+1/2} = dQ_{j+1/2}/dx at x = x_{j+1/2} (2.10). ENO-LLF (Algorithm 2.2): the same construction applied separately to H^{+-}[x_{l-1/2}, x_{l+1/2}] = (1/2)(f(u(x_l)) +- alpha_{j+1/2} u(x_l)) (2.11), with alpha_{j+1/2} = max over u between u_j and u_{j+1} of |f'(u)| (2.12), stencils starting at j for H^+ and j+1 for H^-, fhat_{j+1/2} = sum of the two derivatives (2.13). 'Previous implementation' = the ENO schemes of the authors' earlier report [12], denoted ENO-LF in Remark 2.2(c) (global Lax-Friedrichs splitting f^{+-}); its formula is not printed in this report.

hypotheses.text: 1D scalar nonlinear problem (d = m = 1) for the construction in Sec. 2; extension to systems and multi-D in Sec. 4.

The Euler forward step (1.4) is assumed (not proved) to be total variation stable under a CFL restriction (1.5); 'At present this stability cannot be proven for unmodified third order or higher ENO schemes.'
Algorithm 2.1 (ENO-Roe) 'yields a scheme admitting a stationary entropy-violating expansion shock since it is based on the first order Roe scheme'.
Comparison is supported by 'the numerical experiments of Section 5' (Remark 2.2(d)).

quantifier: these two schemes compared with the earlier ENO-LF implementation; no data class stated
justification: The cost part is argued in Remark 2.2(c): ENO-LLF costs the same as ENO-LF (two divided-difference tables) and ENO-Roe half as much (one table), so 'lower computational cost' holds for ENO-Roe but for ENO-LLF the report itself says the cost is equivalent to ENO-LF. The sharpness and accuracy parts rest on a heuristic viscosity ordering (Remark 2.2(d)) and on numerical experiments only. The same report says ENO-Roe admits a stationary entropy-violating expansion shock, so on transonic-rarefaction data (e.g. Burgers with a stationary expansion jump) ENO-Roe would not be more accurate than an entropy-satisfying scheme; whether the sentence is read as a universal or a typical-case claim decides its truth. Not settled by what we read.

sentence: ENO-RF (Algorithm 2.3) seems preferred, since this method is half as expensive as ENO-LLF or ENO-LF, gives better resolution and seems always to converge to the correct entropy solution.
scheme: Algorithm 2.3 (ENO-RF), Sec. 2: fhat_{j+1/2} is defined by (2.10) (ENO-Roe, Algorithm 2.1) if f'(u) does not change sign between u_j and u_{j+1}; otherwise by (2.13) (ENO-LLF, Algorithm 2.2). See item shu_osher_1988_eno2:01 for (2.4)-(2.13). Associated E-flux (2.17): h^{RF}_{j+1/2} = f(u_j) if f'(u) >= 0 between u_j and u_{j+1}; f(u_{j+1}) if f'(u) <= 0 between u_j and u_{j+1}; h^{LLF}_{j+1/2} = (1/2)[f(u_j) + f(u_{j+1}) - alpha_{j+1/2}(u_{j+1} - u_j)] (2.15) otherwise; the report notes the algorithm 'is not equivalent to the ENO scheme obtained by using h^{RF} as a building block'. Time stepping: r-th order TVD Runge-Kutta (1.6) with CFL lambda <= C_r lambda_0 (1.7b).

hypotheses.text: Euler forward step assumed (not proved) TV stable under a CFL restriction (1.5).
'Numerically we observe that Algorithm 2.3 always yields the correct entropy solution even for nonconvex f. See Section 5 for some examples.'

Cost of Algorithm 2.3 'is very close to that of Algorithm 2.1 because sonic points are isolated'; Algorithm 2.1 is half as expensive as Algorithm 2.2 or ENO-LF (one divided-difference table instead of two).
Theoretical justification of stability is not available: 'theoretical justification for the evident stability of these methods would be quite welcome.'

quantifier: this one scheme; 'always' over initial data and fluxes (including nonconvex) tried
justification: The cost claim is argued in the report (sonic points isolated, so ENO-RF costs about as much as ENO-Roe, which uses one divided-difference table against two). The entropy-convergence claim is hedged ('seems') and supported only by numerical examples (Sec. 2 after (2.17), Sec. 5); no convergence or entropy proof is given, and the report says even TV stability of the Euler forward step is assumed, not proved, for order >= 3. We know of no published counterexample and no proof, so UNSURE.

sentence: Conservation, dissipation, or other solution properties with respect to any convex functional are enforced by the addition of a relaxation parameter that multiplies the Runge–Kutta update at each step.
scheme: ODE (1.1) d/dt u = f(t,u) in a real Hilbert space H; eta: H -> R smooth convex (Sec. 1). RK method (1.4)-(1.5), Sec. 1.2: y_i = u^n + dt sum_j a_ij f(t_n + c_j dt, y_j) (1.5a); u^{n+1} = u^n + dt sum_i b_i f_i (1.5b), f_i = f(t_n + c_i dt, y_i), with A 1 = c. Relaxation (Sec. 2): u^{n+1}_gamma = u^n + gamma_n dt sum_i b_i f_i (2.1), gamma_n a root of r(gamma) = eta(u^n + gamma dt sum_i b_i f_i) - eta(u^n) - gamma dt sum_i b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i> (2.4). Definitions (Sec. 1.2): dissipation preserving if eta(u^{n+1}) <= eta(u^n) whenever <eta'(u), f(t,u)> <= 0 for all u, t (1.2); conservative if eta(u^{n+1}) = eta(u^n) whenever <eta'(u), f(t,u)> = 0 (1.3).

hypotheses.text: Dissipation needs non-negative weights b_i and gamma_n >= 0.
A positive root gamma_n exists only for sufficiently small dt, under sum_{i,j} b_i a_ij > 0, sum_{i,j} b_i (a_ij - b_j) < 0 (true for order >= 2) and eta''(u^n)(f_0, f_0) > 0.
eta is a smooth convex function on a real Hilbert space H; A 1 = c.

quantifier: every convex functional; the RK method and step size are not quantified in the sentence
justification: With hypotheses: Theorem 2.2 (from (2.3): eta(u^{n+1}_gamma) - eta(u^n) = gamma_n dt sum b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i>, which is 0 under (1.3) and <= 0 under (1.2) if b_i >= 0, gamma_n >= 0) and Theorem 2.7 (existence of a positive root for small dt, order >= 2). Read alone, the sentence does not mention that a useful (positive) root need not exist for every RK method or step size: for forward Euler with eta = ||u||^2/2 and f(u) = J u, J skew, r(gamma) = gamma^2 dt^2 ||J u||^2 / 2 has only the root gamma = 0, which does not advance the solution. Whether 'enforced' covers that degenerate case is a reading question, so alone UNSURE.

sentence: Moreover, other desirable stability (such as strong stability preservation) and efficiency (such as low storage requirements) properties are preserved.
scheme: Relaxation RK (2.1) with gamma_n a root of (2.4); see item ranocha_etal_2020_rrk_entropy:01 for (1.5) and (2.4). Direction d = dt sum b_i f_i (2.5) and estimate e = dt sum b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i> (2.6) are computed on the fly, so r(gamma) = eta(u^n + gamma d) - eta(u^n) - gamma e.

hypotheses.text: 'It has been shown in [26, Section 3] that the relaxation modification of many SSP methods retains the same SSP property of the original method as long as gamma_n deviates not too much from unity.'
d and e 'can be computed on the fly during the computation of the Runge–Kutta method and are not influenced by gamma_n. Hence, existing low-storage implementations can be used.'

quantifier: the relaxation modification of RK methods having these properties; which methods is not stated
justification: Low storage: argued in Sec. 2 (d and e need only running sums). SSP: the paper does not prove it; it cites [26, Sec. 3] and restricts it to 'many SSP methods' and gamma_n near 1, which the abstract sentence omits. We did not read [26] for this benchmark (it is a source of an earlier benchmark version), so neither reading is settled by what we read.

sentence: The method defined by (1.5a) & (2.1), where γn is a root of (2.4), is conservative.
scheme: Stages (1.5a): y_i = u^n + dt sum_j a_ij f(t_n + c_j dt, y_j); update (2.1): u^{n+1}_gamma = u^n + gamma_n dt sum_i b_i f_i; gamma_n a root of (2.4): r(gamma) = eta(u^n + gamma dt sum_i b_i f_i) - eta(u^n) - gamma dt sum_i b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i>. Conservative (Sec. 1.2): eta(u^{n+1}) = eta(u^n) whenever <eta'(u), f(t,u)> = 0 for all u in H, t in [0,T] (1.3).

hypotheses.text: eta: H -> R smooth convex; H real Hilbert space; A 1 = c.

quantifier: every RK method, every step size, every root gamma_n of (2.4)
justification: r(gamma_n) = 0 gives eta(u^{n+1}_gamma) - eta(u^n) = gamma_n dt sum b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i> (2.3), and under (1.3) each <eta'(y_i), f_i> = 0, so eta(u^{n+1}_gamma) = eta(u^n). This holds for any root, including the trivial root gamma = 0.

sentence: If the weights bi are non-negative and γn ≥ 0, then the method is dissipation preserving.
scheme: As in item ranocha_etal_2020_rrk_entropy:03: (1.5a), (2.1), gamma_n a root of (2.4). Dissipation preserving (Sec. 1.2): eta(u^{n+1}) <= eta(u^n) whenever <eta'(u), f(t,u)> <= 0 for all u, t (1.2).

hypotheses.text: b_i >= 0 and gamma_n >= 0 (in the sentence).
gamma_n is a root of (2.4).
eta smooth convex on a real Hilbert space.

quantifier: every RK method with non-negative weights, every non-negative root gamma_n, every step size
justification: From (2.3), eta(u^{n+1}_gamma) - eta(u^n) = gamma_n dt sum b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i>; each term is <= 0 under (1.2) when b_i >= 0, and gamma_n dt >= 0. 'The method' refers back to sentence 1 of the theorem (gamma_n a root of (2.4)), which is part of the same statement.

sentence: Let a Runge–Kutta method be given with coefficients such that sum_{i=1}^s b_i a_ij > 0 and let r(γ) be defined by (2.4). If η''(u^n)(f_0, f_0) > 0, then r'(0) < 0 for sufficiently small ∆t > 0.
scheme: r(gamma) (2.4) = eta(u^n + gamma dt sum_i b_i f_i) - eta(u^n) - gamma dt sum_i b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i>, with stages (1.5a) and f_0 = f(t_n, u^n) (1.6). The printed condition reads 'sum_{i=1}^s b_i a_ij > 0' in the text layer; Remark 2.4 identifies it with the second-order condition sum b_i a_ij = 1/2, i.e. a double sum over i and j.

hypotheses.text: sum_{i,j} b_i a_ij > 0 and eta''(u^n)(f_0, f_0) > 0 (in the statement).
eta smooth convex; f expanded as f_i = f_0 + O(dt) in the proof (smoothness of f used, not stated as an assumption).

quantifier: every RK method with the coefficient condition; some sufficiently small dt
justification: Proof printed after the lemma: r'(0) = -dt^2 sum_{i,j} b_i a_ij int_0^1 eta''(...)(f_0,f_0) dv + O(dt^3) (2.9), negative for small dt under the stated conditions (given f smooth enough for the Taylor expansion).

sentence: Let a Runge–Kutta method be given with coefficients satisfying sum_{i,j=1}^s b_i (a_ij − b_j) < 0. If η''(u^n)(f_0, f_0) > 0, then r'(1) > 0 for sufficiently small ∆t > 0.
scheme: r(gamma) as in (2.4) (see item ranocha_etal_2020_rrk_entropy:05); f_0 = f(t_n, u^n).

hypotheses.text: sum_{i,j} b_i (a_ij - b_j) < 0 and eta''(u^n)(f_0, f_0) > 0 (in the statement).
eta smooth convex; Taylor expansion of f_i in the proof.

quantifier: every RK method with the coefficient condition; some sufficiently small dt
justification: Proof printed: r'(1) = -dt^2 sum b_i (a_ij - b_j) int_0^1 eta''(...)(f_0,f_0) dv + O(dt^3) (2.11), positive for small dt; Remark 2.6 notes the sum is -1/2 for second-order methods.

sentence: Assume that the Runge–Kutta method satisfies sum b_i a_ij > 0 and sum_{i,j} b_i (a_ij − b_j) < 0, which is true for all (at least) second order accurate schemes. If η''(u^n)(f_0, f_0) > 0, r (2.4) has a positive root for sufficiently small ∆t > 0.
scheme: r(gamma) (2.4) = eta(u^n + gamma dt sum_i b_i f_i) - eta(u^n) - gamma dt sum_i b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i>; RK stages (1.5a).

hypotheses.text: Coefficient conditions and eta''(u^n)(f_0,f_0) > 0 (in the statement).
eta smooth convex.

quantifier: every RK method of order >= 2 (or with the two coefficient conditions); some sufficiently small dt
justification: Proof printed: r(0) = 0, r'(0) < 0 (Lemma 2.3) so r < 0 just right of 0; r'(1) > 0 (Lemma 2.5) and r convex, so r grows without bound beyond 1 and has a positive root. The clause about second-order schemes follows from the order conditions sum b_i c_i = 1/2, sum b_i = 1 (Remarks 2.4, 2.6).

location: Sec. 2.2, Theorem 2.10 (quoted from the authors' [26, Theorem 2.4])
sentence: Let the given Runge–Kutta method be of order p. Consider the IDT/RRK method defined by (1.5a) & (2.1) and suppose that γn = 1 + O(∆t^{p−1}). 1. The IDT method interpreting u^{n+1}_γ ≈ u(t_n + ∆t) has order p − 1. 2. The relaxation method interpreting u^{n+1}_γ ≈ u(t_n + γn ∆t) has order p.
scheme: Stages (1.5a): y_i = u^n + dt sum_j a_ij f(t_n + c_j dt, y_j); update (2.1): u^{n+1}_gamma = u^n + gamma_n dt sum_i b_i f_i. IDT: u^{n+1}_gamma is taken as the value at t_n + dt. RRK: u^{n+1}_gamma is taken as the value at t_n + gamma_n dt (Sec. 2, after Theorem 2.2).

hypotheses.text: RK method of order p; gamma_n = 1 + O(dt^{p-1}) (in the statement).

quantifier: every RK method of order p; every choice of gamma_n with gamma_n = 1 + O(dt^{p-1})
justification: No proof here (cited from [26]); we checked it directly. Let u_RK = u^n + d, d = dt sum b_i f_i = u(t_n+dt) - u(t_n) + O(dt^{p+1}). IDT: u^{n+1}_gamma - u_RK = (gamma_n - 1) d = O(dt^p), a local error O(dt^p), so order p - 1. RRK: u(t_n + gamma dt) - u(t_n) - gamma (u(t_n+dt) - u(t_n)) = gamma (gamma - 1) dt^2 u''/2 + higher terms with factor (gamma - 1), which is O(dt^{p+1}) when gamma - 1 = O(dt^{p-1}); so the local error at t_n + gamma_n dt is O(dt^{p+1}) and the method has order p (step sizes gamma_n dt stay comparable to dt).

sentence: Let W be a Banach space, ψ : [0, T] × H → W a smooth function, and b_i, c_i coefficients of a Runge–Kutta method of order p. Then sum_{i=1}^s b_i ψ(t_n + c_i ∆t, y_i) = sum_{i=1}^s b_i ψ(t_n + c_i ∆t, u(t_n + c_i ∆t)) + O(∆t^p).
scheme: RK stages y_i from (1.5a) with u(t_n) = u^n; u(t) the exact solution of (1.1).

hypotheses.text: psi smooth; RK method of order p (in the statement).
f smooth enough that the RK method has order p on the extended ODE (2.16) (used in the proof).

quantifier: every smooth psi, every RK method of order p
justification: Proof printed: apply the RK method to the extended ODE phi' = psi(t,u), u' = f(t,u), phi(t_n) = 0 (2.16); order p gives dt sum b_i psi(t_n + c_i dt, y_i) = phi(t_n + dt) + O(dt^{p+1}) (2.17), and the quadrature (b, c) of an order-p RK method integrates the exact psi(t, u(t)) to O(dt^{p+1}) (2.18); dividing by dt gives the claim.

sentence: If η is smooth and the given Runge–Kutta method is p-th order accurate, r(γ = 1) = O(∆t^{p+1}).
scheme: r(gamma) (2.4) = eta(u^n + gamma dt sum_i b_i f_i) - eta(u^n) - gamma dt sum_i b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i>; at gamma = 1, r(1) = eta(u^{n+1}) - eta(u^n) - dt sum b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i> with u^{n+1} from (1.5b).

hypotheses.text: eta smooth; RK of order p (in the statement).

quantifier: every smooth eta and every RK method of order p
justification: Proof printed: Theorem 2.11 with psi = <eta'(u), f(t,u)>, combined with (2.12) (eta(u^{n+1}) - eta(u^n) equals the integral of <eta', f> up to O(dt^{p+1})), gives (2.15), i.e. r(1) = O(dt^{p+1}).

sentence: Assume that the conditions of Theorem 2.7 are satisfied. Hence, there exists a unique positive root γn of r (2.4). Consider the IDT/RRK method defined by (1.5a) & (2.1) and suppose that the given Runge–Kutta method is p-th order accurate. 1. The IDT method interpreting u^{n+1}_γ ≈ u(t_n + ∆t) has order p − 1. 2. The relaxation method interpreting u^{n+1}_γ ≈ u(t_n + γn ∆t) has order p.
scheme: RK stages (1.5a), relaxation update (2.1) with gamma_n the positive root of (2.4); IDT and RRK interpretations as in item ranocha_etal_2020_rrk_entropy:08. Conditions of Theorem 2.7: sum b_i a_ij > 0, sum b_i (a_ij - b_j) < 0, eta''(u^n)(f_0,f_0) > 0, dt sufficiently small.

hypotheses.text: Conditions of Theorem 2.7 (coefficient conditions, eta''(u^n)(f_0,f_0) > 0, sufficiently small dt).
RK of order p.
eta smooth convex.

quantifier: every RK method of order p meeting the conditions; sufficiently small dt
justification: Proof printed: r(1) = O(dt^{p+1}) (Corollary 2.12) and r'(1) = c dt^2 + O(dt^3), c > 0 (proof of Lemma 2.5), so there is a root gamma_n = 1 + O(dt^{p-1}); Theorem 2.10 (checked in item :08) gives the orders. Uniqueness: r is convex with r(0) = 0 and r'(0) < 0; for small dt the segment u^n + gamma d stays near u^n where eta'' (d,d) > 0 by continuity, so r is strictly convex there and has exactly one positive root.

sentence: Suppose that the given Runge–Kutta method is p-th order accurate with p ≥ 2. If ⟨η'(u^{n+1}), sum_i b_i f_i / ‖sum_i b_i f_i‖⟩ = B(u^n) ∆t + O(∆t^2) with B(u^n) ≠ 0, then r (2.4) has a positive root γn = 1 + O(∆t^{p−1}). If this root is used to define IDT/RRK methods by (1.5a) & (2.1), then: 1. The IDT method interpreting u^{n+1}_γ ≈ u(t_n + ∆t) has order p − 1. 2. The relaxation method interpreting u^{n+1}_γ ≈ u(t_n + γn ∆t) has order p.
scheme: As in items :08 and :11; here eta is a general smooth function, not necessarily convex (Sec. 2.3, paragraph before the proposition). The relation symbol before 0 in 'B(u^n) ... 0' is missing in the text layer; we read it as '≠' (the hypothesis is used as a non-degeneracy condition).

justification: The proof is a sketch ('The proof of [7, Theorem 2] using the implicit function theorem can be adapted to this setting'); we did not read [7]. The hypothesis controls <eta'(u^{n+1}), d>, but r'(1) = <eta'(u^{n+1}), d> - e with e = dt sum b_i <eta'(y_i), f_i>, and the sketch does not show how e enters when the problem is not conservative. We could not check the adaptation, and the relation symbol in the hypothesis is not legible, so UNSURE.

sentence: In this paper we have proposed, analyzed, and demonstrated a general approach which allows any Runge–Kutta method to preserve the correct time evolution of an arbitrary functional, without sacrificing linear covariance, accuracy, or stability properties of the original method.
scheme: Relaxation RK (2.1) with gamma_n a root of (2.4) (see item ranocha_etal_2020_rrk_entropy:01), RRK interpretation u^{n+1}_gamma ~ u(t_n + gamma_n dt).

hypotheses.text: Existence of a positive root needs order >= 2 coefficient conditions, eta''(u^n)(f_0,f_0) > 0 and sufficiently small dt (convex case), or the condition of Proposition 2.16 (general case).
Accuracy p is kept by the RRK interpretation; the IDT interpretation loses one order.
SSP retained for 'many SSP methods' only 'as long as gamma_n deviates not too much from unity' (cited from [26]).
Linear invariants are conserved (cited from [26]).

quantifier: every RK method, every functional
justification: Alone FALSE, counterexample: forward Euler (s = 1, b = 1, a = 0), eta(u) = ||u||^2/2, f(u) = J u with J skew-symmetric and u^n with J u^n nonzero. Then e = dt <u^n, J u^n> = 0 and r(gamma) = ||u^n + gamma dt J u^n||^2/2 - ||u^n||^2/2 = gamma^2 dt^2 ||J u^n||^2 / 2, whose only root is gamma = 0; the relaxed step is u^{n+1} = u^n at time t_n + 0, so this RK method cannot be made to preserve the evolution of eta while advancing in time (consistent with Theorem 2.7 needing order >= 2). With the paper's hypotheses (order >= 2, small dt, eta'' condition) the accuracy part holds for RRK (Theorem 2.14), but 'without sacrificing ... stability properties' rests on the cited SSP result restricted to gamma_n near 1, which we did not read; so UNSURE.

sentence: In the case of convex functionals, there are additional insights such as the possibility to add entropy dissipation by the time integration scheme.
scheme: Relaxation update (2.1) with a value gamma in (0, gamma_n), where gamma_n is the positive root of r (2.4) (Remark 2.9).

justification: Remark 2.9: r is convex with roots 0 and gamma_n, so r(gamma) < 0 for 0 < gamma < gamma_n; then eta(u^n + gamma d) - eta(u^n) = gamma e + r(gamma) < gamma e, i.e. extra entropy dissipation beyond the semi-discrete estimate.

sentence: The new approach, combined with an appropriate entropy-conservative/entropy-stable semi-discretization on unstructured grids, yields the first discretization for computational fluid dynamics that is: • Primary conservative • Entropy-conservative/entropy-stable in the fully-discrete sense with ∆t = O(∆x) • Explicit, except for the solution of a scalar algebraic equation at each time step • Arbitrarily high-order accurate in space and time

The priority claim ('first') cannot be checked from what we read. UNSURE.

sentence: A systematic procedure for constructing semidiscrete, second order accurate, variation diminishing, five point band width, approximations to scalar conservation laws, is presented.
scheme: Semi-discrete conservation form (Sec. II, eq. (2.2)): du_j/dt + (1/Delta)(h_{j+1/2} - h_{j-1/2}) = 0, with h Lipschitz and consistent, h(w,...,w) = f(w). Incremental form (2.8): du_j/dt = C_{j+1/2} Delta_+ u_j - D_{j-1/2} Delta_- u_j with C_{j+1/2} = C(u_{j+2}, u_{j+1}, u_j, u_{j-1}) >= 0 and D_{j-1/2} = D(u_{j+1}, u_j, u_{j-1}, u_{j-2}) >= 0, both Lipschitz. Sec. III: start from a three-point first order E scheme h(u_{j+1}, u_j) (Definition (2.1); E schemes are characterized in (2.6) by comparison with the Godunov flux h^G, which is min of f over [u_{j-1}, u_j] if u_{j-1} < u_j and max of f over [u_j, u_{j-1}] if u_{j-1} > u_j); TVD scheme (3.6) adds limited second-order corrections psi(R^{+-}_j) times flux differences, with ratios R^{+-}_j of flux differences (3.5), psi Lipschitz with psi(1) = 1, and the positivity conditions (3.8) on C, D; example limiter (3.9): psi(R) = 0 for R < 0, R for 0 <= R <= k, k for R > k, with 1 <= k <= 2; resulting five-point flux (3.10). Displayed formulas (3.5)-(3.8), (3.10) are largely illegible in the OCR; the description above is from the legible parts and the surrounding prose.

Theorem (3.2): second order accurate except at isolated zeros of h_1(w,w) w_x or h_0(w,w) w_x.
Lemma (2.3): approximation (2.8) is at most first order accurate at nonsonic critical points of u.
Underlying three-point flux h is an E flux, Lipschitz; limiter satisfies (3.8).

With the stated exceptions (Theorem (3.2), Sec. III), second order away from critical points holds since R -> 1 there and psi(1) = 1 with psi Lipschitz; variation diminishing follows from the incremental form with C, D >= 0 (Lemma (2.1) and Sec. II argument); the five-point stencil is explicit in (3.10).

sentence: Good properties of monotone schemes: 1. u_j ≤ v_j for all j (“u ≤ v”) implies G(u)_j ≤ G(v)_j for all j. 2. This immediately implies the Total Variation Diminishing (TVD) property: ‖G(u)‖_BV ≤ ‖u‖_BV.

For 3-point schemes fhat(u_j, u_{j+1}) this holds if fhat is nondecreasing in the first and nonincreasing in the second argument and lambda (fhat_1 - fhat_2) <= 1. The notes' own Cauchy-Schwarz argument (after Theorem 14) allows exactly this equality case ('equality holds only if a and b are linearly dependent', i.e. a single nonzero c_l with l = lambda). sentence: More importantly, for the first time in the finite volume setting, we provide a general proof that the proposed flux limiter maintains high order accuracy of the original WENO scheme for linear advection problems without any additional time step restriction.
